title: Let a connection break before giving its count
reason: Keep the distinction between occupied amount and separate pieces. The exact recorded sequence remains available in a dated note, so it supports the encounter without becoming a list to memorise.

title: Hold a landscape still enough to feel one change
reason: Keep HEIGHT and the signed multiplication in the main text. Move the fixed generator recipe into a note; those constants are useful for returning to the experiment, but do not all need to arrive during the walk.
before: One generator supplies this encounter: OpenSimplex2S, with seed zero, four fBM octaves, gain 0.5 and lacunarity 2. Its frequency is 0.1 and the input coordinates are multiplied by five. Those choices remain fixed while we change HEIGHT. This is one slice through the possibilities of the existing terrain, narrow enough for a difference to become attributable.
after: The seed and the field's other settings stay fixed while HEIGHT changes how much of the same variation reaches the ground. We have held the source still enough to feel what one multiplication changes.[^walk-recipe]

title: Make the controller's limit a bodily question
reason: Keep the forty-five-degree rule because it makes computational permission specific. Move the other measured angles into the dated record, and preserve the distinction between a stalled walk and an impossible landscape.
before: These readings leave work for the body. The section samples a line; your body has width. A capsule can meet a neighbouring slope the line does not touch. A controller's speed, step and slope rules also enter the encounter. The tested desktop body accepts floor angles up to 45 degrees, while route A's steepest sampled segment rises from about 24 degrees at 0.25 to about 58 at 0.90. The measurement helps us investigate the stalled walk without declaring the whole landscape impassable.
after: The section follows a line; your body has width. It can meet a slope beside the line, and its controller brings rules of its own. The recorded desktop body accepted floor angles up to forty-five degrees. Increasing HEIGHT took the steepest sampled stretch of route A from below that limit to above it.[^walk-measurements] That helps us ask why this walk stopped. It does not tell us that no body could pass.

title: Let the coda hold curiosity as well as understanding
reason: The online review values this reflective corridor. My additional editorial concern is its examiner-like voice: name, predict, give your explanation twice, identify, state. Retain observation, explanation and a discriminating experiment, while making space for attachment and an unfinished question.
before:
What can you explain when the busy displays are no longer doing it for you?

The last pair showed why a difference in appearance needs an account of how the pictures were made. This transition asks you to supply that account from one encounter you can remember clearly.

<!-- @dark_sphere -->

Pause where you can see the sphere. Let its slow rotation and changing glow continue while you describe one earlier example. Name the field that supplied values, the positions at which it was sampled, and the way those samples became visible.

Choose a second version in thought. Would changing the threshold alter the same field's classification, or would changing the seed supply different values? Predict one visible consequence of each choice. Use a remembered observation as the reason for your prediction.

Give your explanation twice. First describe only what you saw: a gap widened, a patch changed colour, or a column returned towards its earlier pose. Then describe the operation you think caused it. If the second account introduces a quantity you never observed, identify where you learned about it and what would make it visible. This small separation lets another person follow your reasoning without having to share your first impression of the room.

The sphere is a reference for this pause. It does not present a new noise experiment, and its pulse does not certify that your explanation is correct. A familiar object can help hold attention without measuring what that attention contains.

<!-- @ -->

If two explanations seem possible, keep both for a moment. Name an observation that would distinguish them. You might hold the seed fixed, separate colour from displacement, or compare a direct sample with a displaced sampling coordinate. A useful next action follows from the difference you still need to resolve.

You can also choose what you want to keep from the sequence besides a correct description. Perhaps it is a restless surface, an awkward gap or a route suggested by a ridge. State that attachment without requiring the numerical representation to contain all of it.

The cellular-automata rooms move from a field sampled at positions to states updated through local neighbourhoods. Bring the question of where a value comes from. A point can receive a function's answer, or it can change because of what its neighbours were doing in the previous step.
after:
What has followed you out of the room?

A dark patch that returned with REMAP. A connection that broke when the threshold moved. A ridge that caught your foot. Let one encounter come back before you try to explain the whole sequence.

<!-- @dark_sphere -->

The dark sphere keeps turning. For a moment, there is no new control to learn. Stay with the change you remember. What happened there, before you knew what to call it?

You might begin with what you saw: the patch brightened, the gap widened, the column turned. Then give it another telling, following the operation you learned to recognise. Did a different value arrive, or did the same value find another use?

The two tellings need each other. A name can help us return to what happened; it can also hurry us past something we have not understood. If you are unsure whether a surface changed or only its colour, keep both explanations for a moment. Which small alteration would let you tell them apart?

Hold a seed. Change a threshold. Look at an edge after the veining is gone. One question can give you a reason to return to a room you thought you had finished.

The sphere offers no verdict. Its pulse continues while you choose what to attend to. We have been learning how to make a difference visible, and how much must be held aside for that difference to become clear.

Perhaps what stays with you is the swelling surface itself. You wanted to remain near it, or to make a body that could live in its folds. Knowing its operation gives you something to change. It need not settle what the encounter was worth to you.

<!-- @ -->

In the cellular-automata rooms, a cell's next state will depend on what its neighbours were doing in the previous step. The neighbourhood we have been learning to recognise acquires another task. What kinds of bodies could come from that dependence?

Bring one of your unfinished questions with you.
